title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence & Exceptions
author: Aisha Khan
content:
Purpose

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s authoritative controls and operational workflows for: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC controls, incident response (security), compliance evidence collection, and risk/exception handling. It is intended for engineers, security reviewers, product managers, and compliance owners.

Scope

Applies to: Redwood-hosted control plane and services, Dedicated and Private control-plane components managed by Redwood, and customer-facing admin/console features. Does not replace customer-specific contractual obligations for Dedicated/Private instances where customers manage infrastructure.

1) RBAC & Authentication

Summary
- Principle: Least-privilege by default. All human and machine principals must authenticate and be granted the minimum role(s) required for tasks.
- Primary mechanisms: Single Sign-On (SSO) using OIDC/SAML, short-lived service tokens for automation, and scoped API keys for programmatic access.

Roles and permissions model
- Global roles: admin, security-admin, billing-admin, platform-engineer, support-engineer, read-only, service-account.
- Resource-scoped roles: project-admin, model-deployer, runtime-operator, view-metrics.
- Permission granularity: create/read/update/delete for resources (models, routes, keys, audit-exports), plus action-level permissions (e.g., revoke-key, run-rollout, create-rollback).

RBAC matrix (example)
| Role | Models | Routes | Keys | Billing | Audit Exports | Console UI |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| admin | RW | RW | RW | RW | RW | Full |
| platform-engineer | RW | RW | R | - | R | Operate |
| support-engineer | R | R | - | - | R | Support views |

Authentication & session controls
- SSO: Mandatory for staff. We support IdPs via SAML and OIDC. Enforce 2FA via IdP.
- Service tokens: Issued with explicit expiry (max 90 days) and scope. Long-lived tokens must be rotated every 90 days and recorded in the token registry.
- API keys: Scoped per-project and auditable. Keys created via console must include purpose and owner.

Enforcement & auditing
- All RBAC changes (role assignment, role creation, policy edits) generate high-fidelity audit events (see Audit Logging).
- Periodic role review: quarterly automated report to owners; owners must attest within 10 business days.

2) Audit Logging

Logging requirements
- What to log: authentication events (login, logout, SSO assertions), token creations/revocations, RBAC changes, admin console actions, model deployments and rollbacks, configuration changes (networking, KMS), data access to sensitive stores, and exporter/ingest pipeline changes.
- Minimum fields per event: timestamp (ISO8601 UTC), actor (principal id), actor_type (user/service), action, resource_type, resource_id, outcome (success/failure), request_id, ip_address, user_agent, correlation_id.

Log format example (JSON):
```
{
  "timestamp": "2026-02-10T15:04:05Z",
  "actor": "user:alice@redwood.ai",
  "actor_type": "user",
  "action": "role.assign",
  "resource_type": "project",
  "resource_id": "proj-1234",
  "outcome": "success",
  "request_id": "req-7f9a0",
  "ip_address": "198.51.100.42",
  "user_agent": "console/1.3.2",
  "correlation_id": "corr-55a3"
}
```

Retention and storage
- Immutable, append-only audit store with write-once policy for primary retention window.
- Default retention policy: authentication logs: 2 years; admin/audit logs (RBAC, config changes): 7 years for enterprise customers with compliance requirements; standard logs for most customers: 3 years. Retention is configurable per-customer for Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Storage: encrypted-at-rest (AES-256) and encrypted-in-transit (TLS 1.2+). Access to raw logs limited to security and SRE with Just-In-Time access approvals.

Log access and exports
- Exports: ad-hoc exports are available to owners; exports require approval for restricted datasets. Exports are signed and checksum-verified.
- SIEM integration: native forwarding to customer SIEMs (via secure connector) and to internal SIEM.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Classification
- Data classes: Public, Internal, Confidential, Regulated (e.g., PD, PCI, PHI). Each asset mapped to a class with required controls.

Residency controls
- Controls: region pinning for storage and compute, geo-fencing for backups, and explicit support for customer-requested region-only deployments for regulated customers.
- Default behavior: control plane metadata stored in US or EU regions depending on customer selection. For Dedicated/Private, customers can require on-prem or VPC-only residency.

Retention policy table
| Data type | Default retention | Rationale | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Authentication logs | 2 years | Support investigations & compliance | Security |
| Audit/config change logs | 3 years (standard) / 7 years (enterprise) | Regulatory audits, legal hold | Compliance |
| Model input/output traces (customer opt-in) | 90 days default (configurable) | Cost and privacy | Product/Customer |
| Backups (metadata) | 1 year | Restore capability | Infra |

Data deletion & legal hold
- Deletion requests follow the Data Deletion Procedure (see related page). Legal holds override retention and must be coordinated with Legal; held data is quarantined and flagged in the metadata index.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Development Lifecycle)

Gates & controls
- Security gates in PRs: dependency scanning, static application security testing (SAST) for critical repos, secret scanning, and pre-merge unit tests. Failing a security gate blocks merge.
- CI policies: all production artifacts must be produced by CI pipelines with signed build metadata, SBOM generated for each release, provenance stored in the artifact registry.
- Code review: two approvers required for production-impacting changes; at least one approver from a separate team for cross-team changes.

Developer guidance
- Secrets: no secrets in repo. Use Vault (or equivalent) and environment injection. Secrets must be rotated on detection; incident response notified if secret exposure is in a commit.
- Dependency policy: automatic dependency updates allowed; high/critical CVEs trigger immediate mitigation (patch or compensating control) within 72 hours.

Release & change management
- Rollout pattern: staged (canary → ramp → full) with automated rollback on safety signals. Rollout gating includes: errors spike > 2x baseline for 5 minutes, latency increase > 30% for 5 minutes, or model-quality regression tests fail.

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Incident classification
- Sev definitions: Sev 1 (active data exfiltration / production outage impacting SLAs), Sev 2 (elevated risk: data exposure potential, degraded SLOs), Sev 3 (minor security incidents, low impact).

Detection & triage
- Alerts from SIEM, IDS, customer reports or automated monitors route to Security Pager. Initial triage within 15 minutes for Sev 1/2.

Containment & eradication checklist (example steps)
1. Preserve forensic evidence: snapshot affected hosts, export audit logs and network captures to locked evidence bucket.
2. Isolate affected services or routes (scale-to-zero or firewall block) if needed.
3. Rotate credentials and revoke compromised tokens; require forced re-auth where appropriate.
4. Apply remediation patch or configuration change.
5. Validate remediation via test harness and production smoke tests.

Post-incident
- Postmortem: every Sev1/2 incident requires a written postmortem within 7 business days, including timeline, root cause analysis, corrective actions, and KPTs. Postmortem reviewed by Security, SRE, and Product.
- Communication: incident comms templates are stored in the Incident Playbook; legal and customer-success are engaged for customer-impacting incidents.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Evidence types & owners
- Evidence artifacts: audit logs, role-approval attestations, vulnerability scan reports, SBOMs, SCA reports, architecture diagrams, test results, and signed deployment manifests. Each artifact must include: owner, timestamp, retention policy, and provenance.

Collection process
- Automated collection: CI publishes SBOM and build-signature to evidence-bucket on successful deploy. Security scans push reports to evidence repo.
- Manual evidence: role review attestations and policy signoffs collected via Confluence forms and archived as PDFs in the evidence store.

Packaging for audits
- Pre-built audit packages: per-quarter and per-customer packages assembled automatically for review. Packages include a manifest.json (human-readable summary allowed) with links to artifacts, hashes, and access permissions.

Audit readiness SLA
- Internal audit requests: evidence delivered within 5 business days.
- External audit (customer or regulator): initial evidence package within 10 business days; full cooperation plan determined by Legal and Account teams.

7) Risk & Exceptions

Exception request process
1. Submit exception request via the Exceptions form (link in related pages) with scope, compensating controls, and proposed expiry.
2. Security evaluates risk and assigns TTL (risk acceptance window) and required mitigations.
3. Exceptions requiring >90 days or involving regulated data escalate to CISO and Legal.

Risk acceptance matrix (high level)
- Low: accepted by service owner with compensating control documented.
- Medium: requires Security review and mitigation plan; time-limited approval.
- High: requires CISO approval and periodic re-review (30/60/90 day check-ins).

Periodic review
- All active exceptions reviewed at least quarterly; owners must attest or close. Exceptions auto-expire if not renewed.

Appendix: Quick commands & examples

- Export audit logs (CLI):
```
redwood audit export --project proj-1234 --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-02-01 --format ndjson --out /tmp/audit-export.ndjson
```

- Approvals: Example role attestation CSV header:
```
project_id,role,principal,attestation_owner,attestation_date,status,notes
```
